title: Register Renaming
summary: How mapping architectural registers onto a larger pool of physical registers eliminates false dependences and unlocks more out-of-order reordering.

slides.markdown:
WAR and WAW hazards ([ilp-fundamentals](ilp-fundamentals)) aren't real data dependences, but a naive out-of-order engine still has to respect them: if instruction B writes the same register instruction A later reads (WAR) or writes (WAW), executing B first would leave the wrong value behind.

Without a fix, the hardware must serialize these pairs exactly as if they were true dependences — throwing away reordering opportunity for a conflict that only exists because two instructions happen to share a register name, not because any value actually needs to flow between them.

**Register renaming** maps each **architectural register** (the fixed, ISA-visible names like `R1`) onto a much larger pool of **physical registers** the ISA never exposes. Every time an instruction writes to an architectural register, the hardware allocates it a *fresh* physical register instead of reusing the old one.

The result: two instructions that both happen to write `R1` in the program now write two *different* physical registers. The name collision that caused the WAR/WAW hazard simply doesn't exist anymore at the hardware level — there's nothing left to serialize on.

slides.sectionTitle: Same architectural register, different physical ones
slides.markdown:
![The same architectural register R1, written twice, renamed to two different physical registers P7 and P12](assets/register-renaming.svg)

Both instructions target architectural `R1`, but the rename table assigns the first write `P7` and the second `P12`. A later read of `R1` is redirected to whichever physical register the table says currently holds the right value — the mapping, not the name, is what execution tracks.

slides.sectionTitle: The physical register file and map table
slides.markdown:
Two structures make renaming work: the **physical register file (PRF)**, a pool much larger than the architectural register count (often 100–200+ entries vs. 16–32 architectural), and the **register alias/map table**, tracking the current architectural-to-physical mapping.

On every decode, the map table is consulted for operands' physical registers and updated with the new physical register for the destination — this table is what makes the relabeling possible every instruction, every cycle, without stalling.

| Hazard | Fixed by renaming? |
|---|---|
| WAR (write-after-read) | Yes — different physical registers, no conflict |
| WAW (write-after-write) | Yes — same reasoning |
| RAW (true dependence) | **No** — the true data flow still has to happen in order |

**How to decide:** renaming is not a general parallelism trick — it specifically removes *name* conflicts so the scheduler is free to reorder around them; it does nothing to shorten a genuine RAW chain, which forwarding and scheduling still have to handle on their own.

A common mix-up: **architectural register count** is ISA-visible ([registers-and-register-files](registers-and-register-files)) — RISC-V has 32, x86-64 has 16 general-purpose registers — fixed by the encoding and stable across every implementation.

**Physical register count** is a microarchitecture choice, invisible to software, varying across chip generations — one x86-64 core might have 180 physical integer registers, the next 224, with zero ISA change. Don't cite one as if it were the other, and don't assume a small architectural count limits reordering — renaming decouples the two.
